doc.title: Plas Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996

chapter: Opening and arrival in Los Angeles
title: Arriving in L.A. in the rock and roll era: Otis and Capitol
summary: He and his pianist brother starved for months, then played with Johnny Otis, got R&B dates, and via Dave Cavanaugh recorded for Capitol with Nat Cole, Sinatra and others.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Rock & roll. Rock & roll in the 50s. I played on a lot of the rhythm & blues labels when I first came to L.A. in ‘55 — ‘54, ‘55. and that music was taken over by the rock ‘n rollers. And they I guess they were pop artists, trying to duplicate this music that was so hot with I guess the white teenage buying public at the time.
When you got to L.A. and you maybe — how do you get your first date when you get to a big city and you are an unknown?

You don’t. Unless you’re playing with somebody who is going to make a recording. I’ve played around town. My brother and I got into L.A. around 1954, and you know we were half a band, he is a piano player and I’m a sax player so all you really have to do is find a drummer, and if it’s a real good gig we had a bass player.

But we starved around quite a few months before getting on to something. And I met and played with Johnny Otis. Johnny Otis had his going Rhythm & Blues Revue going at the time, and I played with him a while, and I started getting calls for some rhythm & blues dates. I’m trying to remember the labels now, Modern, Aladdin — and these artists, well actually one of the artists that recorded on these labels was Charles Brown, who I first went on the road with when I was 19 years old, out in New Orleans. It was my bus ticket out of New York was the Charles Brown Band. So you get to know people in the town, when you get to the town, you go around and try to make all the jam sessions and people © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

hear you play and usually people like my playing when I play. And Johnny Otis did some records on Capitol and I had heard at Capitol via Dave Cavanaugh, who was a producer and A&R man out there, and he got me on fabulous recordings with Nat Cole and Frank Sinatra and Peggy Lee and Ella Mae Morse. I forget all the people. Capitol was a hot label at the time.
Yeah, he did some good work with Nancy Wilson.
